cards.front: Reverse proxy vs load balancer vs API gateway
cards.back: A proxy handles HTTP (TLS, compression, caching), a load balancer spreads load over identical servers, and a gateway applies API policy: auth, per-client limits, routing to many services.
Verify the JWT or API key once at the edge, then pass a trusted user ID in a header so services don't each re-implement login.

cards.front: What stays out of the gateway
cards.back: Business logic. The gateway is shared by every team, so a rule specific to one service belongs in that service.
A small service per client type (web, mobile, partners), owned by that client's team, that shapes responses for its screens.
Moves timeouts, retries, mutual TLS, metrics and tracing out of app code into a proxy beside each instance (a sidecar, often Envoy).
An extra proxy hop on every call (about a millisecond), more memory per pod, and a complex control plane to operate.
From the dependency's p99.9 latency, with the caller's timeout longer than the sum of what it waits on.
If the app, sidecar and gateway each retry 3 times, one failing call becomes 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 attempts. Retry at one layer only.
Allow retries up to about 10% of normal traffic, so retries stop adding load when most calls are failing.
After too many failures, stop calling the dependency for a few seconds and fail fast or serve a fallback, then let test requests through before closing.
A separate connection pool per dependency, so one slow service can't use up every connection the caller has.

quiz.q: A bad deploy makes 20% of calls fail and callers retry 3 times. The service, sized for 12k/s at 10k/s normal, melts. What stops the spiral?
choices: A retry budget and circuit breaker
quiz.why: Budgets cap retry load and breakers fail fast, so overload doesn't feed more failures.

quiz.q: A mobile home screen makes three slow round trips to three services. What helps?
choices: Add a CDN for the JSON
Aggregate the calls in a gateway or BFF inside the data center
quiz.why: Inside the data center a round trip is about half a millisecond, so one combined response is much faster.

quiz.q: One slow upstream uses up all gateway workers and every route starts timing out. What prevents this?
quiz.why: Per-route limits keep one bad service from taking the whole API down.

quiz.q: A gateway config change pushed everywhere at once causes a global outage. What is the lesson?
choices: Keep config in version control and roll it out gradually like code
Put business logic in the gateway
quiz.why: Many large outages were one bad config pushed everywhere at once.

quiz.q: You run five services. Do you need a service mesh?
choices: No, a good HTTP client library is usually enough
quiz.why: The mesh's cost pays off at many services; with a handful, a library is enough.

quiz.q: A caller with no timeout on a slow dependency eventually fails too. Why?
choices: Slow calls hold threads and connections until the caller runs out
quiz.why: Without a timeout, waiting calls pile up and exhaust the caller.

quiz.q: Which request is safe to retry automatically after a timeout?
choices: A POST that charges a card with no idempotency key
A read, or a write protected by an idempotency key
Any request, retries are always safe
quiz.why: Retry reads and idempotent writes only; a blind retry of a non-idempotent write can double it.
